dataset_family: Iran Dementia and Alzheimer's Association (IDAA) clients and volunteers, Semnan, Iran (ethics Semnan University of Medical Sciences); analysed at Florida Atlantic University; single site, not public
method_family: Markerless depth-camera instrumented gait (Kinect v2, 50 macro/micro markers) comparing single-task straight vs single-task curve (oval) 10 m walking; group tests per marker plus ROC
what_it_shows: Seifallahi, Galvin & Ghoraani 2024, J Alzheimers Dis Rep 8:423-435 (30 HC vs 25 MCI, same participants in both conditions). In single-task straight walking the macro markers did not differ between MCI and HC (velocity p = 0.780, cadence p = 0.247), but in single-task curve walking they did (velocity p = 0.007, cadence p = 0.018). Straight walking still separated the groups on 20 of 50 micro markers and gave AUC 0.78, against 0.83 for curve walking.
why: Identity: PDF title, authors and DOI 10.3233/ADR-230149 match the block. The extract was read in full; the extractor omits the reference list. PART SHOWN: within the same participants and against a non-impaired comparator, a loaded walking condition separates MCI on the macro gait markers (velocity, cadence, and mean/median step and stride velocity) where the same markers in the unloaded condition do not. That is the shape of the Table A1 claim, with the load coming from path geometry. WHY ONLY PARTLY: (1) The load belongs to none of the three families the statement names. Both conditions are single-task walking, and the authors say the study 'did not incorporate dual-task walking tests'. It bears on the behavioural limb only by analogy, if curve walking is accepted as a 'measure that loads the system'. (2) The unloaded test does separate MCI from HC: 20 of 50 straight-walking markers differ (step and stride length, step height, variability, regularity), and the straight-walking markers give AUC 0.78. So 'the corresponding static measure does not' holds marker by marker for the macro and velocity markers, not for straight walking as a test. The result reads 'loaded is more sensitive' more than 'static fails'. (3) The HC straight-walking velocity SD of 27.92 cm/s is implausible next to the step and stride velocity SDs of about 7 cm/s. However, the straight-walking step and stride velocity nulls (p = 0.574, 0.177) support the velocity null on their own. (4) About 100 marker tests are run with no multiple-comparison correction. The text says Table 2 values were adjusted for BMI (the Methods say BMI, education and GDS), so it is unclear which test produced each p. (5) The groups differ on BMI, education and GDS. (6) The claim that the curve AUC is 'significantly higher' has no test statistic. On the supporting side, the study computes straight-to-curve 'costs' and reports that 13 marker costs differ between the groups, a direct test that the load affects MCI more, but the text does not list which markers. INDEPENDENCE: IDAA, Iran. It shares no cohort, site or author with any current supporter or other candidate. METHOD FAMILY: instrumented loaded gait is in the same broad behavioural 'loaded gait' family as the Guangzhou single/dual-task TUG (P-665/P-687), although the instrument and the load differ. Not a registry duplicate stub. Peer-reviewed, not a preprint. NARROWED: the packet says the record is not a convergence, so n/a.

quotes.quote: In the CW test, we observed signiﬁcant differences between the HC and MCI groups in 27 out of the 50 extracted markers. Among these markers, two were macro markers, namely average velocity, and cadence, while the remaining 25 were micro markers.

Conversely, the SW test revealed signiﬁcant differences in 20 out of the 50 extracted markers. None of these markers were macro markers; instead, they consisted of 5 micro temporal markers, 13 micro spatial markers, and 2 micro spatiotemporal markers.
Speciﬁcally, we noted no signiﬁcant deviations between MCI and HC groups during straight walking when assessing macro gait markers such as average velocity and cadence.
the area under the curve (AUC) for curved path walking (0.83) was signiﬁcantly higher than for straight path walking (0.78)

The costs of 31 out of 50 gait markers (62%) were greater for MCI than HCs when the walking tests changed from SW to CW, and 13 marker costs showed signiﬁcant differences between the two study groups.
While this study primarily emphasized MCI and HC participants and did not incorporate dual-task walking tests or biomarker veriﬁcation for MCI diagnoses
However, the two groups had signiﬁcant differences in body mass index (BMI), years of education, and GDS scores.
The values listed in Table 2 have been adjusted for BMI
